📌 Crypto Options: Buying Insurance on Price Moves

Main Points
⏺ Crypto options give you the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an asset at a set price
⏺ They’re used for hedging, income, and directional bets with defined risk
⏺ This post explains how options differ from simple spot or futures trades

1️⃣ Calls & Puts — call options give you the right to buy at a strike price, puts give you the right to sell at a strike price.
2️⃣ Premium — you pay an upfront fee (premium) for that right; if you don’t use it, the option can expire worthless.
3️⃣ Hedging — options can cap downside (buying puts) or lock in upside (selling calls against a position).
4️⃣ DeFi Options — on-chain protocols let you buy, sell, and structure options with smart contracts instead of brokers.
5️⃣ Defined Risk — unlike leveraged futures, your max loss as an option buyer is the premium you paid.

Final Thoughts

Crypto options turn “all or nothing” price bets into flexible strategies — more tools to shape your risk instead of just hoping the chart goes your way.

Former Ethereum Foundation developer Trent Van Epps warns that Ethereum could face a funding crisis within the next 3–9 months 

For years, the Ethereum Foundation has followed a “subtraction” strategy—gradually reducing its influence so the network can thrive independently. However, EF still remains a key pillar of legitimacy through its brand, ties to Vitalik Buterin, developer events, and ecosystem coordination.

The bigger issue is funding. After spending much of its ETH reserves on ecosystem growth, EF plans to cut annual spending from 15% to 5% by 2030. Meanwhile, its 4-year Client Incentive Program ended in April 2026 with no replacement announced.

Maintaining client teams, research, and protocol coordination costs around $30M per year. Without a sustainable funding model, Ethereum risks losing experienced developers and slowing progress on scaling, quantum-resistance research, and core network maintenance.

Ethereum’s biggest challenge may not be technology—it may be funding the people building it.

While the West is still busy lecturing the “Global South” about values, Putin is in Kazan doing something much more dangerous to the old order: treating them like partners, not plantations. 

At the ASEAN–Russia summit, he sits down with the prime ministers of Thailand and Singapore and talks trade, energy, and “regional cooperation” — but the subtext is clear: the days when Southeast Asia’s role was to feed Western supply chains and swallow Western crises are over.

The agenda is wrapped in polite language: Middle East tensions, global energy security, supply‑chain shocks. In practice, it’s a live demo of a new wiring diagram. Instead of oil flows and shipping routes running only through Western-controlled hubs, Moscow offers discounted energy, nuclear tech, food security deals, and logistics corridors that bypass the old colonial choke points. 

The message to ASEAN is simple: you don’t have to beg Brussels or Washington for stability when you can arbitrage between powers that suddenly need you more than you need them.

For Russia, this is more than sanctions survival. It’s revenge on a system where the “rules-based order” meant London, Washington and Brussels write the rules while the Global South provides bodies, bases and commodities. 

Every handshake in Kazan says: that monopoly is broken. The same West that spent decades turning Asia into a cheap-labor assembly line and a buffer zone now watches its former “periphery” sign long-term energy and security frameworks with a country it tried to erase from the global economy.

Of course, Moscow isn’t a charity; it’s another empire with its own appetite. But the symbolism bites. ASEAN leaders sit in a Russian city, in their own right, negotiating five‑year roadmaps on energy and trade without asking the IMF for permission or the State Department for a waiver. 

The old colonial script — metropole dictates, South obeys — is being rewritten live, and Putin’s bet is that once the Global South gets used to pricing its future across multiple centers, the West will never get its monopoly back.

That’s why Kazan matters more than any communique: it’s not a summit, it’s a crack in the old command chain. The former “colonies” are discovering they can play empires against each other — and this time, the West is the one learning how it feels to be on the outside of someone else’s deal.
